result:
I’ve been thinking lately about how much of life happens in the in-between moments. Not birthdays or graduations, but Tuesday afternoons, sleepy bus rides, reheated coffee. Nobody photographs those hours, yet somehow they hold everything together.

Yesterday I watched an old man in the park feed pigeons like he had all the time in the world. He tore his bread slowly, talked to them softly, laughed when one landed on his bench. For a minute, the rush of emails and headlines and errands just dissolved.

I think joy is often that quiet, unremarkable, gently showing up when you finally slow down. We’re taught to chase big adventures, climb mountains, move cities, change everything at once. But maybe meaning is smaller and closer, hiding in familiar faces and daily rituals.

It’s in the way my sister saves the funny stories to tell me later. It’s in steam rising from soup, neighbors waving, dogs pulling toward every interesting smell. It’s in forgiving yourself for yesterday and starting again without fanfare.

I used to worry I wasn’t doing enough, achieving enough, becoming enough quickly. Now I try to measure a good day differently: Did I notice something beautiful? Did I make someone’s load a little lighter, even just by listening? Did I allow myself to rest without guilt, to wander without destination? If the answer is yes to any of those, I call it enough, I call it full.

Tomorrow will bring its own noise, but today I choose softness and attention. Always.
